title: Предложение Кости и благодарность Шефа  (Kostya's Proposal and the Chef's Gratitude)

segments.t: As the wedding guests wonder why the bartender is singing about Nastya instead of the bride Katya, Kostya drops to one knee and asks Nastya to marry him. Later, while the staff celebrates with champagne, Chef Barinov sincerely thanks Max for saving the day—but still refuses to take him back into the kitchen.
Понял, а почему он поёт про Настю?
Невеста же вроде Кати.
Выйди же за меня.
К веселым конкурсам и шарадам.
У нас есть веселые конкурсы и шарады?
Веселых нет.
А давайте лучше выпьем.
А ты не хочешь поблагодарить Макса?
Да, шеф, Агузок красавец.
Спасибо, Агузок.
Это значит, вы меня простили?
Я могу вернуться?
Я же тебе сказал, не возьму обратно.
Now let's break down each line of their conversation.
Понял, а почему он поёт про Настю?
'Wait, why is he singing about Nastya?' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'understood?' and finishing on 'Nastya'. Chef Viktor answers right away.

'The bride's name is supposed to be Katya.' Notice how Russian expresses 'bride' and 'Katya' with crisp inflection rather than helper words.
Выйди же за меня.
'Will you marry me?' Nastya anchors the line on 'step out', while 'me' completes the thought.
К веселым конкурсам и шарадам.
'Onward to fun contests and charades.' In Russian, the idea of 'cheerful' flows naturally into 'charade' without extra filler words. Chef Viktor answers right away.
У нас есть веселые конкурсы и шарады?
'Do we actually have any fun contests and charades?' The meaning hinges on 'by' working together with 'charade' in spoken Russian.
Веселых нет.
'None that are fun.' The grammar packs 'cheerful' and 'there is no' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange.
А давайте лучше выпьем.
'Let us all have a drink instead.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'and' and finishing on 'will drink'. Chef Viktor answers right away.
А ты не хочешь поблагодарить Макса?
'Do you not want to thank Max for today?' Chef Viktor raises the pitch on 'Max' to turn the phrase into a direct spoken question.
Да, шеф, Агузок красавец.
'Yes, Chef, Oguzok was a real champion today.' The meaning hinges on 'yes' working together with 'handsome man' in spoken Russian.
Спасибо, Агузок.
'Thank you, Oguzok.' Notice how Russian expresses 'thank you' and 'rookie' with crisp inflection rather than helper words. Chef Viktor answers right away.
Это значит, вы меня простили?
'Does that mean you have forgiven me?' Chef Viktor chooses the respectful plural 'you' alongside 'forgave' to keep a polite distance.
Я могу вернуться?
'Can I come back to work?' Notice how Russian expresses 'I' and 'to return' with crisp inflection rather than helper words.

'I already told you, I will not take you back.' Max anchors the line on 'I', while 'back' completes the thought. Now let's put it all back together and hear the whole scene again.
